topic: Attitude, Aptitude & Foundational Values, and Emotional Intelligence

items.title: Attitude — content, structure and functions
items.body:
### What an attitude is, and what it is made of

**In one line**
An attitude is a learned, fairly lasting like-or-dislike towards something — a person, idea, object or situation — and it is built from three parts: feelings, actions and beliefs.

**Why it is asked**
The ABC structure and Katz's four functions are classic one-mark items, and the whole attitude block underpins answers on changing officials' outlook towards transparency and service.

**The story**
An **attitude** is an **evaluative orientation** — a settled favourable or unfavourable stance. Its **content** is simply what it is about; its **structure** is the famous **ABC model**: an Affective part (feelings), a Behavioural part (the tendency to act), and a Cognitive part (beliefs). These three usually line up, which is why attitudes guide behaviour.
**Katz's functional theory (1960)** then asks *why* we bother to hold attitudes at all, and answers with four jobs they do for us — gaining rewards, protecting the ego, expressing our values, and making sense of the world.

**Picture it — the ABC model**

| Component | Meaning | Governance example |
|---|---|---|
| Affective | Feelings and emotions | Discomfort with corruption |
| Behavioural (conative) | Tendency to act | Reporting wrongdoing |
| Cognitive | Beliefs and thoughts | 'Transparency improves trust' |

**Katz's four functions**
- **Adjustment (utilitarian)** — holding the attitude maximises rewards and minimises punishment.
- **Ego-defensive** — it protects self-esteem from anxiety and inner conflict.
- **Value-expressive** — it lets us assert our central values and identity.
- **Knowledge** — it gives structure and meaning to a complex world.

**Terms explained**
- **Evaluative orientation** — a stance that rates something as good or bad for us.
- **Conative** — relating to action or will; the behavioural part of an attitude.
- **Valence** — the direction of an attitude, positive or negative.
- **Centrality** — how core an attitude is to a person's identity; central attitudes resist change and strongly steer behaviour.

**Don't confuse**
- **Attitude vs value vs belief vs opinion** — a value is an abstract ideal (justice); a belief is a factual conviction; an opinion is a value or belief expressed in words; an attitude is the overall like/dislike that may rest on all three.
- **Affective vs cognitive** — feelings versus thoughts; both sit inside one attitude.

**Remember it**
'A-B-C = feel, act, think', and Katz's four = 'reward, defend, express, understand'.

**TL;DR**
- Attitude = learned, lasting evaluative orientation towards an object.
- Structure = ABC: Affective (feel), Behavioural (act), Cognitive (think).
- Katz's four functions: adjustment, ego-defensive, value-expressive, knowledge.
- Strong, central attitudes resist change and strongly guide behaviour.
keyPoints: Attitude = learned, enduring evaluative orientation towards an object, person or idea.
ABC structure: Affective (feelings), Behavioural/conative (action tendency), Cognitive (beliefs).
Distinguish attitude from values (abstract ideals), beliefs (facts) and opinions (verbal).
Katz's four functions: adjustment, ego-defensive, value-expressive, knowledge.
Attitudes vary in valence, strength/centrality and complexity; strong central attitudes resist change.
items.source: NCERT Psychology (Attitudes and Social Cognition); Katz (1960); Britannica — attitude

items.title: Attitude formation, change and the link with thought and behaviour
items.body:
### How attitudes form, change, and (imperfectly) predict behaviour

**In one line**
Attitudes are learned rather than inborn, they shape and are shaped by behaviour, and they predict what we actually do only under the right conditions.

**Why it is asked**
The 'attitude-behaviour gap' (why stated views do not match actions) and cognitive dissonance are favourite concepts for both MCQs and governance case studies on changing officials' conduct.

**The story**
Attitudes are **learned** — through **classical and operant conditioning** (associations and rewards), **observational learning** (copying models), **repeated exposure** and transmission by family, school, peers and media.
Once formed, an attitude shapes how we perceive, remember and interpret things, and disposes us to act. But the **attitude-behaviour link is imperfect**: in **LaPiere's 1934 study**, hoteliers who had actually served a Chinese couple later said in writing they would refuse such guests. Attitudes predict behaviour best when they are **specific, strong and easily brought to mind**, and when situational pressure is weak. Importantly, the arrow runs both ways — **behaviour also changes attitudes**.
Change happens through **cognitive dissonance** (Festinger, 1957), through **persuasion**, and through **direct experience and incentives**.

**Picture it — when attitudes predict behaviour**

| Condition | Effect on prediction |
|---|---|
| Specific attitude | Stronger prediction |
| Strong and accessible attitude | Stronger prediction |
| Heavy situational pressure | Weaker prediction |

**Terms explained**
- **Classical conditioning** — learning by association (a neutral thing paired with a liked/disliked thing).
- **Operant conditioning** — learning by consequences (rewards strengthen, punishments weaken).
- **Cognitive dissonance** — the mental discomfort of holding two clashing thoughts; we reduce it by changing an attitude.
- **Accessible attitude** — one that comes to mind quickly, so it is more likely to steer action.

**Governance relevance**
A professed pro-citizen attitude must translate into responsive behaviour; training and role-modelling can genuinely reshape officials' attitudes towards transparency, gender sensitivity and service.

**Don't confuse**
- **Attitude vs behaviour** — holding an attitude does not guarantee the matching action (the LaPiere gap).
- **Dissonance vs persuasion** — dissonance is internal discomfort driving change; persuasion is an external message driving change.

**Remember it**
'LaPiere = words beat actions'; 'dissonance = discomfort forces a rethink'.

**TL;DR**
- Attitudes are learned via conditioning, observation, exposure and group transmission.
- LaPiere (1934) showed the attitude-behaviour gap.
- Attitudes predict behaviour best when specific, strong, accessible and pressure-free.
- Cognitive dissonance (Festinger, 1957) drives change; behaviour and training can reshape attitudes.
keyPoints: Attitudes are learned via conditioning, observation, exposure and group transmission.
LaPiere (1934) demonstrated the attitude–behaviour gap (stated intent ≠ actual action).
Attitudes predict behaviour best when specific, strong, accessible and free of situational pressure.
Cognitive dissonance (Festinger, 1957) drives attitude change to restore consistency.
Behaviour can reshape attitudes; training/role-modelling can reorient officials' attitudes.

items.title: Moral and political attitudes
items.body:
### Moral attitudes and political attitudes

**In one line**
A moral attitude judges things by right and wrong, a political attitude is a stance towards political objects like the state and parties, and a civil servant must keep private political views out of public duty.

**Why it is asked**
Case studies often set a personal political leaning against the duty of neutrality; examiners want the distinction, the source (political socialisation) and the resolution (serve the Constitution).

**The story**
A **moral attitude** evaluates persons, acts or policies against standards of right and wrong. Because it is anchored in core values (honesty, justice, non-violence), it tends to be **strong and resistant to change**, and for a public servant it underpins **integrity** and the will to resist wrongdoing.
A **political attitude** is an evaluative stance towards **political objects** — the state, the Constitution, parties, ideologies, leaders and policies. It ranges along axes such as **liberal-conservative**, **left-right** and **authoritarian-democratic**. Both kinds of attitude are learned through **political socialisation**: family, school, peers, media, religion and major events transmit them over a lifetime.
The two can clash — for example, loyally implementing a lawful policy you personally dislike. The ethical resolution is to serve the Constitution and the public interest above private preference.

**Picture it — political attitude axes**

| Axis | One end | Other end |
|---|---|---|
| Economic | Left | Right |
| Social outlook | Liberal | Conservative |
| Authority | Democratic | Authoritarian |

**Terms explained**
- **Political object** — anything political an attitude can be about: the state, a party, an ideology, a leader.
- **Political socialisation** — the lifelong process by which people acquire political attitudes.
- **Non-partisanship / neutrality** — not favouring any party while on duty; serving whichever government is lawfully in power.

**Public-service caution**
A civil servant may privately hold political attitudes but must stay non-partisan in duty, so that citizens of every persuasion are served equally.

**Don't confuse**
- **Moral vs political attitude** — moral is about right/wrong; political is about state and parties. A person can be morally firm yet politically neutral.
- **Holding a view vs acting on it** — private political views are allowed; acting partisanly on duty is not.

**Remember it**
'Moral = right/wrong, Political = state/parties; on duty, Constitution outranks preference.'

**TL;DR**
- Moral attitude = evaluation against right/wrong; strong and value-anchored.
- Political attitude = stance towards state, parties, ideologies (liberal-conservative, left-right).
- Both come mainly from political socialisation.
- Civil servants may hold political views privately but must stay non-partisan on duty.
keyPoints: Moral attitude = evaluation against right/wrong; strong, value-anchored, resistant to change.
Political attitude = orientation towards state, parties, ideologies (liberal–conservative, left–right).
Political socialisation (family, school, peers, media) is the main source of political attitudes.
Civil servants may hold political attitudes privately but must stay non-partisan on duty.
Sound moral attitude underpins integrity and resistance to wrongdoing.
items.source: NCERT Political Science (political socialisation); NCERT Psychology

items.title: Social influence and persuasion
items.body:
### How others change us, and how messages persuade

**In one line**
Social influence is the process by which other people change our thoughts, feelings or behaviour, and persuasion is the use of messages to do so — through either careful thought or surface cues.

**Why it is asked**
The named experiments (Asch, Milgram), Kelman's three processes and the two persuasion routes are standard MCQ fodder, and they explain how government behaviour-change campaigns work.

**The story**
There are three classic forms of **social influence**. **Conformity** is yielding to group norms — shown in **Asch's** line experiments — driven by a wish for approval (normative influence) or for accuracy (informational influence). **Compliance** is agreeing to a direct request, nudged by tricks like foot-in-the-door and door-in-the-face. **Obedience** is following authority — **Milgram's** experiments showed how far people will go, which is a warning against unethical 'just-following-orders' conduct. **Kelman** described how influence deepens from compliance (going along) to identification (copying someone admired) to **internalisation** (genuinely accepting the view).
**Persuasion** is explained by the **Elaboration Likelihood Model (Petty and Cacioppo, 1986)**: when people think hard, the **central route** (quality of argument) persuades durably; when they do not, the **peripheral route** (surface cues) persuades only briefly.

**Picture it — the two persuasion routes**

| Route | Basis | Durability |
|---|---|---|
| Central | Effortful scrutiny of argument quality | Lasting, predicts behaviour |
| Peripheral | Surface cues (credibility, attractiveness, repetition) | Transient |

**Terms explained**
- **Normative influence** — conforming to be liked or accepted.
- **Informational influence** — conforming because others seem to know better.
- **Foot-in-the-door** — a small request first makes a bigger one easier to grant.
- **Door-in-the-face** — a big request first makes a smaller follow-up easier to grant.
- **Internalisation** — truly adopting a belief as your own, not just obeying.
- **Elaboration** — how much mental effort a person puts into weighing a message.

**Governance use**
Behaviour-change communication (immunisation, sanitation, tax compliance) works best through credible messengers and the central route; officials must also recognise manipulation and resist it.

**Don't confuse**
- **Compliance vs internalisation** — compliance is outward agreement that fades; internalisation is genuine, lasting acceptance.
- **Central vs peripheral route** — the central route changes attitudes durably; peripheral cues change them only briefly.

**Remember it**
'Asch = conform, Milgram = obey, Kelman = comply/identify/internalise'; 'central = think, peripheral = cue'.

**TL;DR**
- Influence forms: conformity (Asch), compliance (foot-in-the-door), obedience (Milgram).
- Conformity is driven by normative (approval) and informational (accuracy) influence.
- Kelman: compliance → identification → internalisation.
- ELM (Petty and Cacioppo): central route = argument (durable); peripheral = surface cues (transient).
keyPoints: Social influence forms: conformity (Asch), compliance (foot-in-the-door), obedience (Milgram).
Normative vs informational influence explains why people conform.
Kelman's three processes: compliance, identification, internalisation.
ELM (Petty & Cacioppo): central route = argument scrutiny (durable); peripheral = surface cues (transient).
Persuasion factors: source credibility, message quality, audience motivation/ability.
Behaviour-change governance campaigns work best through credible messengers and the central route.
items.source: Asch (1951); Milgram (1963); Kelman (1958); Petty & Cacioppo (1986); NCERT Psychology

items.title: Aptitude and foundational values for civil service
items.body:
### Aptitude and the foundational values of a civil servant

**In one line**
Aptitude is the capacity to learn and do a job, and foundational values are the ethical bedrock — integrity, impartiality, objectivity, empathy and more — expected of every public servant.

**Why it is asked**
The exact list of foundational values (from the Second ARC and UPSC's framework) and the Nolan principles are directly quotable in answers and appear as matching-type MCQs.

**The story**
**Aptitude** is the natural or acquired capacity to learn and perform a role; **civil-service aptitude** blends analytical ability with the temperament and values that public office demands. On top of ability sit the **foundational values** — the ethical qualities a public servant must have so that legal authority becomes legitimate, humane and trusted governance. The **Nolan Committee (UK)** adds an allied, widely cited list, the Seven Principles of Public Life.

**Picture it — foundational values**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Integrity | Wholeness; consistency between values and action; incorruptibility |
| Impartiality | Fairness among persons and interests, without favour |
| Non-partisanship | Political neutrality; serving the government of the day without party bias |
| Objectivity | Decisions on evidence and merit, not personal bias |
| Dedication to public service | Citizens' welfare placed above self-interest |
| Empathy | Understanding citizens' feelings and situations |
| Tolerance | Respect for diverse views, faiths and identities |
| Compassion | Care for the suffering, especially weaker sections |

**Terms explained**
- **Aptitude** — the ability or readiness to learn and perform a particular kind of work.
- **Impartiality** — treating all persons and interests even-handedly.
- **Non-partisanship** — not taking a party side; serving whichever government is lawfully elected.
- **Weaker sections** — groups historically disadvantaged (poor, SC/ST, persons with disability, etc.) who need special care.
- **Nolan principles** — the UK's seven standards for public life.

**Nolan's Seven Principles**
Selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership — these convert legal authority into legitimate and trusted governance.

**Don't confuse**
- **Aptitude vs attitude** — aptitude is capacity to do the work; attitude is the like/dislike stance you bring to it.
- **Impartiality vs non-partisanship** — impartiality is fairness among people; non-partisanship is neutrality among political parties.

**Remember it**
Nolan's seven = 'SI-OA-OHL' (Selflessness, Integrity, Objectivity, Accountability, Openness, Honesty, Leadership).

**TL;DR**
- Aptitude = capacity to learn/perform; civil-service aptitude blends ability with ethical temperament.
- Integrity = values match action; impartiality = fairness without favour; objectivity = evidence-based.
- Non-partisanship = political neutrality; empathy, tolerance and compassion humanise administration.
- Nolan's seven: selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership.
keyPoints: Aptitude = capacity to learn/perform; civil-service aptitude blends ability with ethical temperament.
Integrity = consistency of values and action; impartiality = fairness among persons without favour.
Non-partisanship = political neutrality; objectivity = evidence/merit-based decisions.
Dedication to public service = citizens' welfare above self-interest.
Empathy, tolerance and compassion (esp. towards weaker sections) humanise administration.
Nolan Committee's Seven Principles: selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership.
items.source: Second ARC, 4th & 10th Reports; Nolan Committee (UK) Seven Principles of Public Life

items.title: Emotional intelligence in administration and governance
items.body:
### Emotional intelligence and its use in governance

**In one line**
Emotional intelligence is the ability to perceive, understand, manage and use emotions — your own and others' — and it makes administrators both effective and humane.

**Why it is asked**
Goleman's five components, the Salovey-Mayer origin and the governance uses are standard MCQ and essay content, and EI versus IQ is a common trap.

**The story**
**Emotional intelligence (EI)** is the capacity to perceive, understand, manage and use emotions in oneself and others. The term was coined by **Salovey and Mayer (1990)** and popularised by **Daniel Goleman (1995)**, whose model has **five components**. In governance, EI shows up as composure in crises, skill in resolving conflict, warmth in service delivery, strength in leading teams, and resilience against the emotional pressures behind corruption. EI **complements** (it does not replace) domain knowledge and legal competence, and it is distinct from **IQ**.

**Picture it — Goleman's five components**

| Component | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Self-awareness | Recognising one's emotions and their impact |
| Self-regulation | Managing impulses and moods; staying calm under pressure |
| Motivation | Inner drive to achieve beyond money or status |
| Empathy | Sensing and considering others' feelings |
| Social skills | Building rapport and managing relationships and teams |

**Terms explained**
- **Emotional intelligence (EI)** — handling emotions wisely in yourself and others.
- **IQ** — intelligence quotient; reasoning and problem-solving ability, which EI is separate from.
- **Self-regulation** — keeping impulses and moods in check.
- **Empathy** — understanding what another person is feeling.

**Utilities in governance**
- Crisis and stress management (disasters, law and order) with composure.
- Conflict resolution and negotiation with stakeholders.
- Empathetic, citizen-centric service delivery, especially for vulnerable groups.
- Team leadership and motivation of subordinates.
- Ethical resilience — resisting manipulation, anger and the temptations behind corruption.

**Don't confuse**
- **EI vs IQ** — IQ is reasoning ability; EI is emotional skill. High IQ does not guarantee high EI.
- **Coined vs popularised** — Salovey and Mayer coined the term (1990); Goleman popularised it (1995).

**Remember it**
Goleman's five = 'self-aware, self-regulate, motivate, empathise, socialise'.

**TL;DR**
- EI = perceive, understand, manage and use emotions (self and others).
- Term coined by Salovey and Mayer (1990); popularised by Goleman (1995).
- Goleman's five: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills.
- Governance uses: crisis management, conflict resolution, empathetic delivery, leadership, ethical resilience; EI is distinct from IQ.
keyPoints: EI = perceive, understand, manage and use emotions (self and others).
Term coined by Salovey & Mayer (1990); popularised by Goleman (1995).
Goleman's five components: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills.
Governance utilities: crisis/stress management, conflict resolution, empathetic delivery, team leadership, ethical resilience.
EI complements (not replaces) domain knowledge and legal competence; distinct from IQ.
items.source: Salovey & Mayer (1990); Daniel Goleman, Emotional Intelligence (1995); Second ARC, 10th Report
